children: Morgan Stanley
is pushing back against one of the bond market's biggest fears, arguing that America's rapidly expanding debt load is a poor guide to where Treasury yields are headed. The call comes as the
10-year Treasury yield approaches 4.8%
, its highest level since early 2025, and suggests investors should focus less on headline debt figures and more on
inflation, economic growth and Federal Reserve policy
The numbers are nonetheless daunting. The Congressional Budget Office projects federal debt held by the public will rise from roughly
101% of GDP in 2026 to 120% by 2036
, before reaching an unprecedented
. Net interest costs alone are projected to climb from 3.3% of GDP this year to 4.6% in 2036.
Morgan Stanley's counterargument is historical. The U.S. has added roughly
$9 trillion of public debt since October 2022
, yet 10-year yields remain around levels seen during that period. That weak relationship suggests debt issuance alone cannot explain bond-market moves.
Instead, the bank expects inflation eventually to return toward the Fed's
2% target
, reducing the need for persistently restrictive monetary policy. CBO's own baseline similarly assumes inflation eases toward 2% by 2030 and projects the 10-year yield at roughly
, remaining relatively stable thereafter.

The immediate market backdrop is less friendly. Rising oil prices and hawkish signals from Fed Chair Kevin Warsh have pushed traders toward expectations of another rate hike, driving a global bond selloff.
Investors Takeaway
For holders of long-duration Treasury funds such as
TLT
and
TLH
, the critical variables are now
core inflation, payroll growth, oil prices and Fed expectations
, rather than debt milestones alone.

Cooling inflation or weaker employment could pull yields lower and boost long-duration bond prices. Persistent inflation, however, would weaken Morgan Stanley's thesis in the near term by keeping Fed policy tighter and term premiums elevated.
The larger takeaway is that America's debt problem remains serious, but for Treasury investors,
the timing of inflation and monetary-policy shifts may matter much more than the absolute debt total

title: Morgan Stanley Says U.S. Debt Fears Miss Bigger Story
